title: Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes (2011)
summary: The proposed nationwide employment class lacked the required common proof, and individualized backpay did not fit the requested Rule 23(b)(2) class.
notes:
Additional assigned discussion appears at printed pp. 831–833 and 849. The Court left open whether some incidental monetary relief could accompany a Rule 23(b)(2) class; it did not hold that every form of money relief is categorically unavailable. Compare Mosley’s different Rule 20 question.

The proposed class was about 1.5 million current and former female employees across roughly 3,400 stores; Justice Scalia wrote for a 5–4 majority on commonality, which "requires the plaintiff to demonstrate that the class members 'have suffered the same injury'" and that the common contention is "capable of classwide resolution."

sections.Parties: Female Wal-Mart employees sought to represent roughly one and a half million women alleging sex discrimination in pay and promotion.
sections.Material Facts: The proposed class spanned thousands of stores and a large number of local managerial decisions. The employees relied on statistical differences, accounts of discriminatory treatment, and expert discussion of a corporate culture said to permit stereotyping. Wal-Mart delegated substantial pay and promotion discretion to local managers and maintained a formal policy against discrimination. The central dispute was whether the proof connected those varied decisions to a common discriminatory mode of exercising discretion.
sections.Procedural History: The district court certified the class and the Ninth Circuit largely upheld certification. The Supreme Court reversed. Five Justices found the commonality showing inadequate; all Justices agreed that the backpay theory did not support certification under Rule 23(b)(2).
sections.Issue: Did the proposed class satisfy commonality, and could the requested individualized backpay be pursued in the injunctive class category?
sections.Holding: No on the showings made. The plaintiffs lacked the required common basis for resolving the discrimination claims together, and the individualized backpay claims did not fit Rule 23(b)(2).
sections.Reasoning: The majority required a common contention capable of generating a common answer important to the validity of the claims. Merely sharing a protected characteristic or alleging violation of the same statute did not suffice. The statistical and anecdotal materials did not, in the majority’s view, establish the necessary connection across the many local decisions, and the expert evidence did not show how often stereotyping affected them. A policy allowing discretion did not itself identify a uniform discriminatory practice. Separately, the Court explained that Rule 23(b)(2) concerns relief operating on the class as a whole; individualized backpay determinations implicated the protections of Rule 23(b)(3), including notice and opt-out rights. A proposed formula could not remove the employer’s substantive defenses to individual claims.

learning.why: The proposed nationwide employment class lacked the required common proof, and individualized backpay did not fit the requested Rule 23(b)(2) class.

topics.cp-commonality: The plaintiffs needed a common contention whose resolution would answer a question central to the claims together.
topics.cp-class-certification: Certification required rigorous examination of the proposed common proof, even when it overlapped the merits.
topics.cp-rule23b2: Claims for individualized backpay could not be certified under Rule 23(b)(2) on the theory presented.
topics.cp-judicial-discretion: Local managerial discretion was the challenged practice, while judicial certification discretion remained bounded by Rule 23.
topics.cp-frcp-23: The decision construes both Rule 23(a)(2) and Rule 23(b)(2) and is the leading text on both.
topics.cp-predominance: Ginsburg's dissent charged the majority with importing Rule 23(b)(3) predominance concerns into the commonality inquiry.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Ginsburg, joined by three Justices, disagreed with the commonality analysis. She regarded the alleged combination of centralized culture and delegated discretion as a common question and criticized importing predominance concerns into Rule 23(a)(2). Those Justices agreed with the treatment of the requested backpay under Rule 23(b)(2).

mnemonic.rationale: A million and a half women
